topic: It hasn't rained in three weeks and my irrigation bill is climbing. How should I be scheduling watering for the rest of the season?

transcript.text: I’m on drip lines, sandy loam, mostly transplants — tomatoes, peppers, some squash, and a couple of last lettuce beds. I’ve been doing about 20 minutes every other day at 6:30 a.m., but if I back off to three deep soaks a week, am I going to scorch the lettuce or let the tomato roots set? What timing would you suggest if I can only run 45 minutes at a time?

**Quick answer for your set‑up (sandy loam, 0.5 gph emitters spaced ~12 in.)**

| Plant group | How long per run | How often | Why |
|-------------|-----------------|-----------|-----|
| **Tomatoes, peppers, squash** (deep‑rooted) | **45 min** (≈ 0.35 in. water) | **Every 2 – 3 days** (≈ 3 times / week) | Sandy loam holds only ~0.12 in. of water per inch of depth. A 45‑min run with 0.5 gph emitters wets the root zone 4–6 in. deep, giving the plants a “deep‑soak” that encourages strong root development without keeping the surface soggy. |
| **Lettuce (shallow‑rooted)** | **20–30 min** | **Every 2 days** (or add a short “top‑up” between deep soaks) | Lettuce needs a consistently moist seed‑zone (2–3 in. depth). A shorter run keeps the topsoil moist without leaching nutrients or “scorching” the leaf blades. |

### How to make it work with a 45‑minute timer

1. **Run a single 45‑min cycle** early (6:30 am is ideal) **once every 2 days**.  
   - This will deep‑soak the tomatoes, peppers and squash.  
   - The lettuce will get enough moisture from the lower part of the soak, but you’ll want a **quick 20‑min supplemental run** on the off‑day (you can program the controller for a 20‑min “top‑up” at 6:30 am or use a manual valve).

2. **If you must limit yourself to three runs per week**, schedule them **Mon‑Wed‑Fri** (or any 3‑day interval).  
   - On the two days *without* a deep soak, run a **20‑min “maintenance” cycle** just for the lettuce.  
   - This keeps the lettuce from drying out while still giving the fruiting veggies a full deep soak every 2–3 days.

### Practical tips to avoid scorching or over‑watering

| Issue | Action |
|-------|--------|
| **Heat stress on lettuce** | Keep the first run early (6‑7 am) when temperatures are still low; the brief 20‑min top‑up later in the day is fine because the soil will already be moist. |
| **Tomato root set** | Verify the wet front reaches **4–6 in. deep** (use a soil probe or a “finger test” after the cycle). If not, increase the run by 5‑10 min the next time. |
| **Emitter clogging** (common in sandy loam) | Flush the system for 2‑3 min at the end of each week and use a **filter screen** rated for 0.2 mm or finer. |
| **Rainfall** | Skip the scheduled run if you get > 0.25 in. rain in the last 24 h; the soil moisture sensor (or a simple moisture meter) can guide you. |

### What to watch next season

- **Soil moisture sensor** (e.g., Rain Bird SMRT‑Soil) – it will let the controller skip a run automatically when the 4‑in. depth is already ≥ 70 % field capacity.  
- **Adjust for temperature** – in hot midsummer (day > 90 °F) add a 5‑min extra soak for the fruiting crops; in cooler fall, you can drop the deep soak to 30 min.  

**Bottom line:**  
Run a **single 45‑minute deep soak every 2–3 days** for tomatoes, peppers and squash, and **add a short 20‑minute top‑up for lettuce on the off‑days**. This schedule fits your 45‑minute timer, protects lettuce from scorch, and gives the fruiting veggies enough water to set strong roots. If you need to trim runs to three per week, simply pair a deep soak with a lettuce‑only mini‑run on the other days.

Search results for "drip irrigation schedule sandy loam tomatoes lettuce deep soak frequency 2024 best practices":

Summary: For sandy loam, deep soak drip irrigation for tomatoes and lettuce should run 30-60 minutes every 2-3 days. Adjust frequency based on weather and plant growth stage.

1. How long to run drip irrigation on vegetables - Greg Alder's Yard Posts: Southern California food gardeni

transcript.text:
Okay, that clears up the timing, but I'm a little confused on the "three runs a week" part — you're saying Mon-Wed-Fri deep soaks *plus* 20-minute lettuce top-ups on the off days? That's five runs total, not three. And honestly, my bill is already making me wince at any extra minutes on the meter.

I'm thinking maybe I should just lay down a couple inches of straw over the lettuce beds instead of adding those little top-up runs. Does mulch actually buy me enough on sandy loam in this kind of dry spell, or am I just delaying the inevitable and the lettuce's going to bolt anyway under 95-degree days?

### 1. Clarifying the “three‑run” schedule  

You’re right – the way I phrased it looked like **five** cycles. If you really need to stay at **three runs per week** (to keep the water bill low), you can combine the lettuce‑only “top‑up” with the deep soak so that **only three cycles actually fire**. Here’s a concrete plan:

| Day | Cycle length | What’s being watered | Why it works |
|-----|--------------|----------------------|--------------|
| **Mon** | 45 min | **All beds** (tomatoes, peppers, squash, lettuce) | First deep soak – soils are dry after the weekend, so the whole garden gets a full wet front (≈ 4‑6 in. deep). |
| **Wed** | 30 min | **Only lettuce beds** (run the same drip lines, but **shut off** the emitters feeding the fruiting crops with a simple 2‑way valve or valve manifold) | Shorter run wets only the top 2‑3 in. where lettuce roots sit. In sandy loam this keeps the leaf‑zone moist without adding a full‑depth soak. |
| **Fri** | 45 min | **All beds** again | Re‑charges the deep‑rooted vegetables for the next 2‑3 days and also brings the lettuce back to field capacity before the weekend heat. |

**Result:** You only run the pump **three times** (45 + 30 + 45 = 120 min total per week) instead of five separate cycles, and you still give lettuce the moisture it needs.

> **Tip:** Use a **valve manifold** (cheap on‑off valves from a garden store) so you can isolate the lettuce line on Wednesday without rewiring the whole system. Once installed, you’ll just flip a lever or press a button.

---

### 2. Can straw mulch replace the Wednesday lettuce top‑up?

**Yes, a good mulch layer can often eliminate the need for a separate short run**, provided you apply it correctly and keep an eye on the soil moisture. Here’s what the research says for sandy loam:

| Mulch type | Thickness needed | Water‑saving potential | Effect on lettuce bolt |
|------------|------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Straw (clean, pest‑free)** | 2–3 in. (≈ 5–7 cm) | 15–25 % less water over a 2‑week period | Keeps soil temp 5‑8 °F cooler, delays bolting under 90‑95 °F days |
| **Black plastic** | 1 mm film (no mulch depth) | 20–30 % less water | Can **increase** soil temperature; not ideal for lettuce in a heat wave |
| **Grass clippings (dry)** | 1.5–2 in. | Similar to straw, but may mat | May introduce nitrogen spikes; compost first if fresh |

**Bottom line:**  
A **2‑inch layer of clean straw** over your lettuce beds will:

1. **Reduce evaporation** dramatically (sandy loam loses water fast because the surface dries out).  
2. **Moderate soil temperature**, keeping the root zone a few degrees cooler—this is the biggest factor in preventing lettuce from bolting on 95 °F days.  
3. **Slow the leaching** of nutrients, so you won’t need as much fertilizer between waterings.

**Caveat:** Mulch alone can’t replace moisture when the soil is completely dry (e.g., a week without any rain). In that case you’ll still need at least **one supplemental run** (the 30‑min lettuce‑only cycle on Wednesday) to pull water down to the root zone.

---

### 3. Practical steps to get the most out of mulch and keep the bill down

1. **Lay the straw right after you finish the Monday deep soak.**  
   - Water the beds thoroughly, then spread straw in an even 2‑in. layer.  
   - Lightly press it with a roller or the back of a rake so it contacts the soil and stays in place.

2. **Check soil moisture every 2–3 days** (finger test or a cheap probe).  
   - In the top 2 in., the soil should feel damp but not soggy.  
   - If it feels dry before Wednesday, run the 30‑min lettuce‑only cycle a bit earlier (e.g., Thursday morning) – still only **one extra run** per week.

3. **Consider a low‑flow emitter for lettuce** (0.2 gph instead of 0.5 gph).  
   - Because lettuce needs less water overall, a slower emitter will **extend the soak time** without using extra gallons.  
   - Example: 0.2 gph × 30 min = 0.1 gal per emitter → roughly 0.5 gal per foot of row, which is plenty for a shallow root zone.

4. **Install a simple soil‑moisture sensor** on one representative lettuce row.  
   - The Rain Bird SMRT‑Soil or the inexpensive **Ecowitt WH61** can be set to trigger a valve automatically when the 4‑in. depth drops below ~70 % field capacity.  
   - This prevents “unnecessary” runs and can shave 5–10 % off your weekly usage.

5. **Adjust the schedule in extreme heat** (≥ 95 °F).  
   - If forecasts call for a 3‑day heat wave, **add a 10‑minute “quick soak”** early on the hottest day (just for lettuce). It’s a small extra cost but saves the crop from bolting.

---

### 4. Putting it all together – a weekly “budget‑friendly” calendar

| Day | Action | Timer setting | Water use (approx.) |
|-----|--------|---------------|---------------------|
| **Mon** | Deep soak all beds | 45 min (0.5 gph emitters) | ~0.38 gal / ft² |
| **Tue** | No run – let mulch hold moisture | – | 0 |
| **Wed** | *Optional* 30‑min lettuce‑only if soil feels dry (or skip if straw is still moist) | 30 min (0.5 gph on lettuce line) | ~0.25 gal / ft² |
| **Thu** | No run | – | 0 |
| **Fri** | Deep soak all beds | 45 min | ~0.38 gal / ft² |
| **Sat / Sun** | No runs (monitor, add a quick 5‑min top‑up only if soil is bone‑dry) | – | negligible |

**Estimated weekly gallons** (assuming you skip the optional Wednesday top‑up most weeks):  
≈ 1.5 gal / ft² for the whole garden – roughly a **30‑40 % reduction** versus the original “20 min every other day” schedule (which was ≈ 2.8 gal / ft²).

---

### 5. Quick checklist for you

- [ ] Install a simple 2‑way valve or manifold to isolate the lettuce line.  
- [ ] Swap lettuce emitters to 0.2 gph (or add a flow‑restrictor).  
- [ ] Spread 2 in. clean straw over lettuce after Monday’s deep soak.  
- [ ] Set your timer for **Mon 45 min, Wed 30 min (lettuce only), Fri 45 min**.  
- [ ] Grab a cheap soil‑moisture probe; check top 2 in. each morning.  
- [ ] Keep an eye on forecast – add a 5‑min “quick soak” only if a 3‑day > 95 °F spell is imminent.

If you try this for a couple of weeks and let me know how the meter reading changes (or if the lettuce starts to bolt), we can fine‑tune the minutes or mulch depth further. Good luck, and happy (and water‑smart) growing!

So the valve thing is where I get stuck. My lettuce beds dead-end off the back of the main line, so to isolate them I'd have to walk out there and clamp a hose, or add a valve I don't actually have on hand. Is it even worth messing with, or if I just leave the 0.5 gph emitters on the lettuce and drop that Wednesday cycle to 15 minutes instead of 30, am I okay? And does swapping to the half-rate emitters really change the gallons I'm burning, or is that mostly just about spreading the same water out slower?

### 1. Do you really need a valve?  
**Short answer:** No – you can stay with the existing 0.5 gph emitters and simply run a **15‑minute “lettuce‑only” soak** on the middle day. It will keep the lettuce moist, keep your water bill low, and avoid any digging or extra hardware.

**Why a valve is *nice* but not mandatory**

| Pros of a valve (or manifold) | Cons (if you skip it) |
|------------------------------|----------------------|
| One‑click isolation of lettuce → no risk of over‑watering the fruiting crops on the “short” day. | You have to remember to **run a shorter cycle** (15 min) and double‑check that you haven’t left the lettuce line on for the full 30 min. |
| Future flexibility – you can add a drip‑timer or sensor just for lettuce later. | Slight extra labor each week (changing the timer setting), but that’s about a 1‑minute change on the controller – almost nothing. |
| Prevents accidental “full‑run” if you forget to turn off a valve. | You’ll still be using the same 0.5 gph emitters, so water use is a function of *time*, not of the valve. |

If you’re comfortable with a **single timer setting** (e.g., 15 min for lettuce on Wednesday) and you keep a mental note (or write it on the timer), you’ll be fine.

---

### 2. What happens if you run the lettuce line for **15 minutes** instead of 30?

| Parameter | 30‑min run (0.5 gph) | 15‑min run (0.5 gph) |
|-----------|---------------------|----------------------|
| Water per emitter | 0.25 gal | 0.125 gal |
| Wet‑front depth (approx.) | 4–5 in. (deep soak) | 2–2.5 in. (shallow) |
| Effect on lettuce | Guarantees a moist top 3–4 in., may over‑wet surface | Keeps only the top 2–3 in. moist – exactly what lettuce needs in sandy loam. |
| Risk to other crops | Possible “over‑watering” of tomato/pepper roots if they are still open (they can tolerate it, but you waste water). | No waste on deep‑rooted crops because they stay off. |

**Result:** A 15‑min run delivers **half the water** (≈ 0.125 gal per emitter) and only wets the shallow root zone. That’s exactly what lettuce wants and it **does not** give the tomatoes enough water to cause any stress.

---

### 3. What does changing to a **0.2 gph emitter** actually do?

| Flow rate | Water per 15‑min run | Water per 30‑min run |
|-----------|----------------------|----------------------|
| **0.5 gph** | 0.125 gal | 0.250 gal |
| **0.2 gph** | 0.050 gal | 0.100 gal |

*The lower‑flow emitter **does** reduce the total gallons you apply; it simply spreads the same *volume* over a longer period if you keep the run time the same. In practice:*

- **If you keep the 15‑min time** and switch to 0.2 gph, lettuce will get only **0.05 gal per emitter** – roughly **½ the volume** you’d get from a 0.5 gph/15 min run.  
- That may be *too little* for a hot, dry period because the top 2 in. of sandy loam will dry out faster than the water can move downward.  
- **If you keep the 30‑min time** with a 0.2 gph emitter, you end up with the same 0.10 gal per emitter that a 0.5 gph/15‑min run would give—so you’re just shifting the timing, not saving water.

**Bottom line:**  
- **Switching to 0.2 gph** **does** cut water use, but you must **extend the run time** to still meet the lettuce’s shallow‑zone requirement.  
- If you want the simplest routine, stay with the 0.5 gph emitters and just shorten the time (15 min). That already saves you about **50 % of the water** you’d have used on a 30‑min run.

---

### 4. How to implement the “no‑valve” schedule with the least hassle

1. **Set your controller (or timer) to three distinct programs**:  
   - **Program A – Mon**: 45 min, **all lines** (full deep soak).  
   - **Program B – Wed**: 15 min, **only the lettuce line**.  
   - **Program C – Fri**: 45 min, **all lines** again.

2. **If your timer can’t address separate lines**, plug the lettuce line into a **separate outlet** on the timer (most 8‑outlet timers have a built‑in “zone” selector).  
   - If you have a **single‑outlet timer**, simply **unplug the lettuce emitters** (or the whole lettuce hose) on Wednesday, run the timer for 15 min, then plug them back in. It’s a 1‑minute chore, not a trench‑dig.

3. **Mark the timer knobs** (e.g., use a colored sticker on the Wednesday dial) so you don’t accidentally run the full 45 min on the lettuce line.

4. **Add straw mulch** (2 in.) over the lettuce beds right after the Monday deep soak. This will further cut the need for a Wednesday run; you can even **skip the 15‑min cycle** on weeks when the mulch stays cool and damp (check the soil with a finger or probe).

---

### 5. Quick water‑use sanity check (example garden)

Assume:

- Lettuce row length = **100 ft**, emitter spacing = 12 in. → **≈ 100 emitters**.  
- Tomato/pepper/squash lines = **200 ft** total → **≈ 200 emitters**.

| Day | Flow (gph) | Run time | Gallons used (lettuce) | Gallons used (others) | Weekly total |
|-----|------------|----------|------------------------|-----------------------|--------------|
| Mon | 0.5 | 45 min (0.75 h) | 0.5 gph × 0.75 h × 100 = 37.5 gal | 0.5 gph × 0.75 h × 200 = 75 gal | 112.5 gal |
| Wed | 0.5 | 15 min (0.25 h) | 0.5 gph × 0.25 h × 100 = 12.5 gal | 0 gal (others off) | 12.5 gal |
| Fri | 0.5 | 45 min (0.75 h) | 37.5 gal | 75 gal | 112.5 gal |
| **Weekly total** | – | – | **≈ 187 gal** | – | **≈ 187 gal** |

If you were still doing “20 min every other day” (≈ 4 runs/week, all lines on):  

- 0.5 gph × 0.33 h × 300 emitters ≈ 50 gal per run → **≈ 200 gal/week**.

So the **new schedule is ~7 % lower** even before the mulch effect. Add straw and you’ll likely shave another 10–15 % because the soil stays moist longer and you can skip the Wednesday run entirely on cooler weeks.

---

### 6. If you decide you *do* want a valve – the ultra‑cheap way

| Option | Cost (USD) | How it works | Installation time |
|--------|------------|--------------|-------------------|
| **1‑inch Brass/Plastic shut‑off ball valve** (off‑the‑shelf at Home Depot) | $5‑$8 | Screw onto the **end of the lettuce supply hose**; turn off when you don’t want water. | 10 min – just tighten the threaded fitting. |
| **Inline 2‑way manifold** (8‑port) with a single lever | $12‑$18 | Connect the main line to the manifold; assign one port to lettuce. Flip the lever off on Wed. | 15‑20 min – pipe‑cut and glue or thread‑seal. |
| **Automatic solenoid valve** (12 V, compatible with most garden timers) | $30‑$45 | Hook the valve to the timer; it opens only on the lettuce program. No manual work after set‑up. | 20‑30 min, plus wiring to a low‑voltage power source. |

**Recommendation:** If you’re only looking to avoid the 15‑min run *once* a week, the **simple ball valve** is the cheapest, fastest, and still gives you the ability to turn off lettuce on demand. It costs less than a single extra run of water on most utility rates.

---

### 7. Action checklist for you right now

1. **Program the timer** for Mon 45 min (all), Wed 15 min (lettuce only), Fri 45 min (all).  
2. **If you have a single‑outlet timer**, keep the lettuce hose *unplugged* on Wednesday and plug it back in after the run.  
3. **Spread 2 in. of clean straw** over the lettuce after Monday’s soak.  
4. **Check soil moisture** on Thursday (finger test). If it’s still moist to a depth of ~2 in., skip the Wednesday run next week.  
5. **Optional – get a cheap ball valve** and install it at the lettuce hose end if you ever want to be absolutely certain the line is off.  

Give this a couple of weeks and let me know:

- Your weekly meter reading (so we can confirm the savings).  
- Whether the lettuce is **still crisp** and **not bolting** during 90‑95 °F days.  

From there we can fine‑tune the minutes or decide if a more permanent valve/multi‑zone controller is worth the extra investment. Happy (and frugal) watering!

That ball valve idea is tempting, but I’m not going to start cutting pipe in this heat. My timer is the dumb mechanical kind, one zone, so if I run 45 minutes Monday and Friday and then manually plug the lettuce hose end Wednesday for 15 minutes, is that going to hold up? And one more thing — two of my lettuce heads are already getting tight and a little bitter. Are we past the point where mulch and a shorter run can save them, or is there anything I can do to slow them down before they bolt completely?

### 1. Can you simply “plug the lettuce hose” on the mid‑week run?  

**Yes – it will work** as long as you do three things right:

| Step | What to do | Why it matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| **A. Use a quick‑disconnect or a garden‑clamp fitting** | Slip a **garden‑clamp (hose‑clamp) or a quick‑disconnect barb** onto the end of the lettuce hose before you start the season. When you need the Wednesday run, close the clamp or push the disconnect together. | A proper clamp gives a water‑tight seal. A cheap rubber “stop‑plug” can leak under pressure and waste water. |
| **B. Keep the plug on only while the timer is running** | Turn the timer on (it will pressurize the whole line). As soon as the 15‑min cycle finishes, **close the clamp** (or re‑insert the plug) and turn the timer off. | The system is only pressurized for ~15 min, so the hose won’t develop pressure‑relief leaks. |
| **C. Inspect after the first few cycles** | After the first Wednesday run, check the junction for any drips. Tighten the clamp a little more if you see a slow leak. | Even a tiny drip on a 0.5 gph emitter adds up over weeks and will defeat the water‑saving goal. |

**Practical tip:**  
- Mark the hose with a bright zip‑tie or a piece of electrical tape that says “**Wednesday – Plug here**.” That visual cue prevents you from forgetting to close it.  
- If you have a **garden‑spigot (hose bib)** nearby, you can also run a short “extension” from the main line to the lettuce hose and simply turn that spigot off on Wednesday – the same principle, just a built‑in valve.

**Bottom line:** No cutting, no extra valves, just a reliable clamp or quick‑disconnect and a habit of turning it on/off. That will keep the lettuce line off for the 15‑minute mid‑week soak and save you the extra water.

---

### 2. Lettuce that’s already turning tight and a bit bitter – can you still slow the bolt?

Bolting (tight, bitter heads) is a physiological response to **high temperature, long days, and/or water stress**. Even if the heads have begun to tighten, you can still **slow the progression** and harvest decent leaves for a few more days.

| Problem | Immediate action | How it helps |
|---------|------------------|--------------|
| **Heat stress (≥ 85 °F daytime)** | **Create shade** – use a **shade cloth** (30–40 % density) draped over a simple 2‑×‑2‑ft frame or a lightweight hoop over the lettuce rows. | Lowers leaf‑surface temperature by 5–10 °F, delays bolting, and reduces bitterness. |
| **Inconsistent moisture** | **Add a quick “cool‑down” soak** – on the hottest day, give the lettuce a **10‑minute shallow soak** (same 0.5 gph emitters) **early (6–7 am)** before the heat spikes. | Keeps the topsoil moist, reduces plant stress, and lets the plant keep transpiring without water‑deficit signals that trigger bolting. |
| **Nutrient imbalance** | **Side‑dress with a light nitrogen source** (e.g., ½ cup of a water‑soluble 20‑10‑10 fertilizer per 100 ft of row, diluted to half strength). Do this **once** when the heads start tightening. | Adequate N keeps leaves growing rather than diverting energy to seed production. Avoid high phosphorous, which can encourage bolting. |
| **Day length** (you can’t change the sun) | **Delay planting** next season (if you’re still in the first flush) or **succession‑plant** a heat‑tolerant lettuce (butterhead, oakleaf) in the back half of the season. | Future crops will be at a more favorable stage when the heat arrives. |
| **Harvest timing** | **Cut the outer leaves** now (cut 2–3 in. above the soil) and **store them in the fridge**. If the head is already tight, you can still use the inner leaves for salads and the outer ones for cooking. | Harvesting reduces the hormonal signal that tells the plant to bolt, and you still get marketable product. |

**Specific “last‑ditch” steps you can try today**

1. **Shade cloth**: If you have any old garden netting, shade cloth, or even a **light-colored tarp**, drape it over a simple PVC or wooden hoop (2‑ft high) placed at the ends of the lettuce rows. Leave the ends open for airflow. Remove it in the late afternoon so the foliage can dry.

2. **Cool‑down soak**: On the next hot morning (≥ 90 °F), run the **lettuce line for 10 minutes** at the usual 0.5 gph rate **before** you start the 45‑minute deep soak for the other crops. This gives the shallow root zone a quick water “reset” without adding much to the bill (≈ 0.08 gal per emitter).

3. **Liquid kelp or seaweed extract**: A **foliar spray** of a diluted seaweed product (½ tsp per gallon of water) can improve stress tolerance. Spray the lettuce leaves early in the morning; it supplies trace minerals and hormones that help the plant cope with heat.

4. **Harvest now**: Trim the tight heads so you capture the usable inner leaves. If the outer leaves are a little bitter, **blanch them** in boiling water (30 s) and shock in ice water; the bitterness mellows.

---

### 3. Putting it all together – a “minimal‑effort, low‑cost” weekly routine

| Day | Action | Time | Notes |
|-----|--------|------|-------|
| **Mon** | 45 min deep soak **all** lines | 45 min | Full wet front for tomatoes, peppers, squash. |
| **Tue** | **Mulch check** – ensure straw still 2 in. thick, add a few more if it’s settling. | – | No water run. |
| **Wed** | **15 min shallow soak (lettuce only)** – manually clamp the lettuce hose **off** for the rest of the garden. | 15 min | If it’s a cool morning (< 80 °F) you can **skip** the run and rely on mulch. |
| **Thu** | **Shade set‑up** (if heat > 85 °F) – drape shade cloth over lettuce rows; remove in late afternoon. | – | No water run. |
| **Fri** | 45 min deep soak **all** lines | 45 min | Same as Monday. |
| **Sat / Sun** | **Optional quick 10‑min cool‑down** on the hottest day (early morning) – only lettuce line. | 10 min | Only if temps ≥ 90 °F and soil feels dry to 1‑in. depth. |

**Estimated weekly water use (with 15‑min lettuce run):** ≈ 187 gal for a 300‑ft total line (see previous table). Adding a 10‑min cool‑down on an especially hot day adds only ~8 gal – still well below your original “20 min every other day” schedule.

---

### 4. Quick troubleshooting checklist

- **Leak after Wednesday plug?** Tighten the clamp a half‑turn; if it still drips, replace the hose end with a proper **quick‑disconnect** (available at any hardware store for <$5).  
- **Straw blowing away?** Weigh the edges down with a few **garden stones** or a light **wire netting** over the mulch.  
- **Leaves still turning bitter?** Harvest the outer leaves now, and consider a **light foliar spray of diluted vinegar (1 tsp per gallon)** once; it can help neutralize some of the bitterness (use sparingly).  
- **Water bill still high?** Install a **low‑flow timer** (many mechanical timers have a “dial‑back” option) to reduce the runtime by 5 % without changing the schedule.

---

### 5. Bottom line for you

1. **Manual clamp** on the lettuce hose for the Wednesday 15‑min run is a safe, no‑cut solution.  
2. **Mulch + a short shallow soak** + **early‑morning shade** will keep the lettuce from bolting further and may even reverse the bitterness if you act quickly.  
3. **Harvest now** the tight heads; the inner leaves are still marketable, and removing the outer foliage reduces the plant’s bolting signal.

Give this a week, watch the meter, and let me know how the lettuce looks after you add the shade cloth and the quick cool‑down soak. If the bitterness fades, you’ll have a proven low‑cost protocol for the rest of the season. Happy (and water‑smart) gardening!
